entities.name: Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, emerged as a pivotal figure in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, bridging the revolutionary ideals of America and France. Born into French nobility in 1757, Lafayette, driven by Enlightenment principles and a desire to aid the American cause against Great Britain, became a major general in the Continental Army at just 19 years old. His unwavering commitment to liberty and constitutionalism positioned him as a transatlantic symbol of republicanism and a "Hero of Two Worlds," influencing political thought across continents.

Lafayette volunteered for the Continental Army in 1777, quickly earning the trust of General George Washington and distinguishing himself at battles like Brandywine and the winter encampment at Valley Forge. He commanded American troops with skill and courage, playing a crucial role in the decisive Siege of Yorktown in October 1781, which secured American independence. Upon his return to France, Lafayette became a leading voice for reform, serving in the Assembly of Notables and the Estates-General. He presented an early draft of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in 1789 and commanded the National Guard during the initial phase of the French Revolution.

Despite his early revolutionary zeal, Lafayette's commitment to constitutional monarchy led to his imprisonment during the radicalization of the French Revolution. Released in 1797, he remained a steadfast liberal, returning to public life under the Bourbon Restoration and advocating for democratic reforms. His involvement in the July Revolution of 1830, which installed Louis-Philippe as a constitutional monarch, solidified his enduring legacy as a champion of liberty and national self-determination, inspiring subsequent generations of revolutionaries and reformers.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lafayette's pivotal military contributions to the American Revolution secured independence for the United States, while his early leadership in the French Revolution shaped its initial liberal phase. His enduring legacy as a "Hero of Two Worlds" profoundly influenced transatlantic republican ideals and diplomatic relations for centuries.
